headline: A trust anchor list published as RFC 5914 drives path validation, constraints and all.
summary: RFC 5914 is the IETF's interchange format for a trust anchor: not a certificate, but the anchor's key and the constraints a root program otherwise states out of band, the namespace it is trusted for, the policies it may assert, and how far below it a path may run. The toolkit read two vendor formats and not this one. It now reads and writes it, and RFC 5937 section 3.2 says how each constraint reaches RFC 5280 section 6.1 validation: the stricter of the anchor's value and the caller's always wins, so an anchor may narrow what a caller asked for and never widen it.

Added: `pki.schema.trustanchor.parse(input, caps?)` reads an RFC 5914 `TrustAnchorList` into `{ anchors }`, each entry naming which of the three `TrustAnchorChoice` arms it came from in `kind`: `certificate`, `tbsCert` (a bare `TBSCertificate`, an anchor having no signature to check) or `taInfo`. `parseInfo` reads a bare `TrustAnchorInfo`. `pemDecode` and `pemEncode` carry the `TRUST ANCHOR LIST` label, and `pki.schema.parse` detects and routes the format.

A `taInfo` entry is `{ version, pubKey, keyId, taTitle, certPath, exts, excludedExtensions, taTitleLangTag }`. `certPath` carries the anchor's name and its constraints: `policySet`, `policyFlags`, `nameConstr` and `pathLenConstraint`. Every rule RFC 5914 states is enforced: an empty `taName`, a `policySet` carrying policy qualifiers, a negative `pathLenConstraint` and a `requireExplicitPolicy` with no `policySet` are each refused, and where `certPath` carries a certificate its subject, its public key and its `subjectKeyIdentifier` must match `taName`, `pubKey` and `keyId`. The four extension types section 3 excludes from `exts` are listed in `excludedExtensions` and left out of `exts`, because the RFC ignores them rather than refusing the anchor.

`pki.trust.parseTrustAnchorList(input, opts?)` turns a list into the trust-store entries `pki.trust.anchor` takes, the same shape `parseCertdata` and `parseCcadbCsv` produce, so a published list drives `pki.path.validate` without being mapped by hand.

`pki.path.validate` applies an RFC 5914 anchor's constraints as RFC 5937 section 3.2 states. The anchor's name constraints intersect the caller's permitted subtrees and union its excluded ones, its `policySet` intersects `opts.userInitialPolicySet`, each of its `policyFlags` may turn the matching `initialExplicitPolicy` / `initialPolicyMappingInhibit` / `initialAnyPolicyInhibit` on and never off, and its `pathLenConstraint` bounds the path. An anchor can only narrow what the caller asked for, which is what makes the format's "always enforced" safe to apply.

`pki.trustanchor.build(spec, opts?)` writes the list a root program publishes, with `opts.pem` for the PEM form. Every rule the parser enforces is enforced here, so the toolkit does not emit an anchor it would refuse to read, and the result round-trips through the parser before it is returned. The `version` is not a field a caller sets: v1 is the ASN.1 DEFAULT and DER omits it, so each v1 anchor has one encoding.
Changed: `pki.trust.anchor` keeps an entry's `purposes` as `null` where the entry states it as `null`, rather than reading it as a set granting nothing. A store that lists a root and grants it no purpose still produces the all-false set, which is what `pki.path.validate` requires `opts.checkPurpose` to judge; a format carrying no purpose bits at all, such as an RFC 5914 anchor, now says nothing instead of saying "trusted for no purpose". An entry that omits `purposes` altogether is unchanged and still defaults to all-false.
Fixed: An option supplied as a non-enumerable own property now reaches the code that acts on it. Every verb accepted such an option and some then skipped it, with nothing reported. Two of them let a check pass that should have failed: `pki.webauthn.verifyAssertion` ignored an `expectedRpId` written that way and reported the assertion valid against the wrong relying party, and an `opts.tpmPolicy.objectAttributes` entry went unchecked in `pki.webauthn.verify`. The rest changed what was produced or refused: `pki.attrcert.sign` left the named extension or attribute out of the certificate it signed, `pki.crmf.build` left the control out of the request, and `pki.cmp.session` answered that no enrollment arm or support operation had been named, or classified an `ir` request as central key generation.

The same read now applies wherever the toolkit copies or enumerates an object it was handed: `pki.path.validate`, `pki.trust`, `pki.cms.verify`, `pki.cmc`, `pki.est`, `pki.ocsp`, `pki.acme`, `pki.ct`, `pki.scep`, `pki.smime`, `pki.webauthn` and the WebCrypto algorithm surface. It covers the response an `opts.transport` returns, so a `Location`, `WWW-Authenticate`, `Retry-After` or `Content-Type` field a custom transport defines non-enumerably is now found. A caller passing plain objects sees no change.

In `pki.path.validate`, an anchor carrying any RFC 5914 constraint could accept a path that the same call without the anchor refused, because the caller's `initialExplicitPolicy`, `initialPolicyMappingInhibit`, `initialAnyPolicyInhibit` and `userInitialPolicySet` were re-read from a copy that kept only the enumerable ones. The caller's options are now read where they were passed.

A trust anchor's own `basicConstraints` `pathLenConstraint` now bounds the path below it, as RFC 5937 section 3.2 requires of a basic constraints extension associated with the anchor. It applies wherever the anchor states one: a certificate passed to `pki.path.validate` or `pki.trust.anchor`, the `exts` of an RFC 5914 `TrustAnchorInfo`, and that anchor's `certPath.pathLenConstraint`. Where two of them state a limit, the lower applies. **A path that runs deeper than an anchor certificate's `pathLenConstraint` allows is now refused where it previously validated.** Check the certificates in your trust store for a `pathLenConstraint` if you validate chains with intermediates.

`pki.trustanchor.build` refuses a malformed nested record with its own `trustanchor/bad-input` error. A `null` or non-object `taInfo`, `certPath` or `certPath.policyFlags` raised a native `TypeError` from the first field read below it.

Parsing no longer writes a decoded field through an accessor planted on `Object.prototype`. Every format parser builds its record in the schema engine by the field names its structure declares, and those writes reached the prototype chain: a getter-only `signatureAlgorithm`, `issuer`, `extensions` or any other declared name made an ordinary `pki.schema.x509.parse` of a valid certificate throw a native `TypeError`, and a setter took the decoded value instead of the record.
